n1.text: Week 1. 8:40pm. The ninth floor is dark except for your monitor and the glow from the corner office.

n2.text: Marcus appears at the edge of your desk with two takeaway teas and the expression of a man who did not expect company.

n3.speaker: Marcus
n3.text: You're new. New people go home at six and pretend they don't check email. What's keeping you?

choices.text: 'The handover file has a broken formula. I couldn't leave it.'
'Honestly? Trying to impress you.'
'Could ask you the same thing.'

fix.speaker: Marcus
fix.text: ...So did I, three years ago. I just never fixed it. That's on me. Show me.

honest.speaker: Marcus
honest.text: Bold thing to say to your manager in week one. Wrong method, though. Sleep impresses me more than overtime.

same.speaker: Marcus
same.text: Fair. Fifteen years of habit. The building's quieter after eight. I think better when nobody needs anything from me.

tea.text: He sets one of the teas down by your keyboard. It isn't a gesture he makes a show of. He just does it.

n9.speaker: Marcus
n9.text: Go home. That's an instruction, not advice. ...And the formula thing. That's solid.

n10.text: He goes back to his office. The light stays on long after you leave.

n1.text: Week 2. The office coffee machine is making a noise like a dying jet engine. Marcus is crouched in front of it, sleeves rolled, losing.

n2.speaker: Marcus
n2.text: Don't say anything. I have a master's degree. I've run teams of forty. This machine is beating me in front of a junior.

choices.text: Kneel down and help him take the back panel off.
'Should I call facilities, or let you keep your dignity?'
Quietly hand him the manual from the drawer.

help.text: Ten minutes, one exploded filter and a lot of laughing later, it works. He has coffee grounds on his very expensive cuff.

tease.speaker: Marcus
tease.text: Facilities, please. My dignity left at 'dying jet engine.' ...You're funny. Nobody told me you were funny.

manual.speaker: Marcus
manual.text: There's a manual. Of course there's a manual. Don't tell Zara. She'll put it in the team newsletter.

talk.speaker: Marcus
talk.text: I used to be the one who fixed things myself. Somewhere along the way I became the one who sends emails about things being fixed.

choices.text: 'You could still be both.'
'Sounds lonely, up in the corner office.'

both.speaker: Marcus
both.text: Maybe. Don't spread that around. I have a reputation for being unreadable to protect.

lonely.speaker: Marcus
lonely.text: ...That's a very direct thing to say to your boss. It's also not wrong. Let's leave it there.

out.text: He hands you the first cup from the resurrected machine. It's terrible. You both drink it anyway.

n1.text: Week 3. Your first one-to-one. Marcus has printed your work. Printed it. With notes in the margins, in very neat handwriting.

n2.speaker: Marcus
n2.text: Your analysis is sharp. Your slides are a crime scene. Both are fixable. Which do you want first?

choices.text: 'The crime scene. Hit me.'
'What would you do differently, in my seat?'

slides.speaker: Marcus
slides.text: Twenty-three bullet points on one slide. Twenty-three. I counted twice because I didn't believe it. One idea per slide. Make them hungry for the next one.

seat.speaker: Marcus
seat.text: In your seat? I'd ask more questions out loud. You have good ones. You keep them in your notebook like they're contraband.

q.text: There's a pause at the end. The kind where a meeting could end, or something else could start.

choices.text: 'Can I ask you something that isn't about work?'
'Thank you. Same time next month?'

personal.speaker: Marcus
personal.text: ...You can ask. I may not answer. I'm your manager, and there's a line, and I'm usually very good at standing on the right side of it. Go on.

n9.text: You ask why he stayed fifteen years. He looks at the window for a long time.

n10.speaker: Marcus
n10.text: Because the work mattered, and then because I was good at it, and then because leaving felt like admitting the first two weren't enough. That's more than I meant to say.

proper.speaker: Marcus
proper.text: Same time next month. Bring fewer bullet points.

close.text: You leave with a page of margin notes. At the bottom, in the same neat hand: 'Good start. Keep going.'

n1.text: Week 4. After the all-hands. Marcus's door is open, which it never is when he's angry. He's angry.

n2.speaker: Marcus
n2.text: Vaughn wants the Lighthouse team cut by two after launch. He wants me to pick the names. He wants it 'by Friday, discreetly.'

n3.speaker: Marcus
n3.text: ...I shouldn't be telling a junior this. Forget I said it.

choices.text: 'I won't repeat it. But you can't carry that alone.'
'Is my name on that list?'
'Then don't pick. Make the case that the team is the product.'

carry.speaker: Marcus
carry.text: I've carried worse alone. But... thank you. It's strange, hearing someone worry about me in this building.

list.speaker: Marcus
list.text: There is no list yet. And you'd be the last name on it, not that I'm supposed to say that either. Stop making me say things.

case.speaker: Marcus
case.text: ...That's not a bad argument. Write it up. Not for me — for Vaughn, with your name on it. Brave people get noticed.

end.text: When you leave, he closes the door behind you. Through the glass you see him sit very still, then pick up the phone.

n1.text: Week 5. After work. You head up to the rooftop for air and find Marcus on a bench, tie off, phone face down beside him.

n2.speaker: Marcus
n2.text: My sister's getting married. Tonight. In another city. I'm here because Vaughn moved the launch review to tomorrow morning.

n3.speaker: Marcus
n3.text: I told her I'd watch the video. She said, 'You always watch the video, Marcus.' She's right. I'm a world-class video watcher.

choices.text: Sit down next to him and say nothing for a while.
'There's a late train. Go. I'll cover the review prep.'
'You chose the job. That's allowed. Just make sure it's still a choice.'

sit.text: The city hums below. After a while he laughs, quietly, at nothing.

n6.speaker: Marcus
n6.text: Fifteen years and I can't remember the last time someone just sat with me. Everyone wants a decision. You just... stayed.

go.speaker: Marcus
go.text: You'd do that? ...No. I can't let a junior stay up all night so I can go dance at a wedding. But the fact you offered — I'll remember it.

choice.speaker: Marcus
choice.text: Is it still a choice? I genuinely don't know. That frightens me more than Vaughn does.

end.text: For the first time, he isn't unreadable at all. He looks tired, and a little lonely, and very human.

n1.text: Week 6. Vaughn intercepts you in the meeting room, all charm and expensive watch.

n2.speaker: Vaughn
n2.text: I'll be quick. Marcus is a good man, sentimental about his team. I need someone close to him to tell me what he's planning before he plans it. Help me, and the lead role gets a lot less competitive.

choices.text: 'No. And I'm going to tell Marcus you asked.'
'I'll think about it.' Then quietly warn Marcus anyway.
'What exactly would you need?'

expose.speaker: Vaughn
expose.text: ...Brave. Unwise. We'll see how brave you feel in Week 10.

n5.text: You walk straight into Marcus's office and tell him everything. He listens without blinking, then forwards one email to HR and one to the CFO.

n6.speaker: Marcus
n6.text: You understand you just picked a side against a senior director. For me. ...Nobody's done that before. Thank you. Now go — and stay out of rooms alone with him.

quiet.text: You give Vaughn a non-answer. That evening you leave a note on Marcus's keyboard: 'Vaughn is asking about you. Be careful.'

n8.speaker: Marcus
n8.text: Found your note. Unsigned, but your handwriting is as bad as your early slides. Thank you. I owe you one.

spy.speaker: Vaughn
spy.text: Smart. Just small things. Who he meets. What he says about the cuts. Nothing that would hurt anyone.

n10.text: It feels like it hurts someone already.

end.text: Marcus waves at you through the glass on your way out. You don't quite manage to wave back.

n1.text: Week 7. The launch review runs until 11pm. The rain is biblical. You and Marcus end up sharing the last taxi.

n2.text: The city smears past the window. Neither of you is talking about work. You haven't for twenty minutes.

n3.speaker: Marcus
n3.text: I need to say something, and then I need you to help me be sensible about it.

n4.speaker: Marcus
n4.text: I look forward to our one-to-ones more than I should. I find reasons to walk past your desk. I'm your manager. That's not a small thing. It's the whole thing.

choices.text: 'Then we wait until it isn't the whole thing.'
'I feel it too. I don't care about the org chart.'
'You're right. Let's keep it professional.'

wait.speaker: Marcus
wait.text: ...Wait. Yes. That's the sensible answer, and it's also the kind one. You keep doing that. Being both.

n7.text: He doesn't touch your hand. He doesn't need to. The taxi stops outside your building, and he says goodnight like it costs him something.

push.speaker: Marcus
push.text: You should care. I have to. If anything happened while I sign off your reviews, everything you earn here gets a question mark next to it. I won't do that to you.

n9.text: He says it gently. It doesn't land gently.

close.speaker: Marcus
close.text: Thank you. You're right. I'm sorry I made it awkward.

end.text: Monday he is exactly, perfectly professional. It's what you asked for. It still feels like a door closing quietly.

n1.text: Week 8. A rumour reaches the ninth floor: someone saw you and Marcus get into a taxi together. Someone, it turns out, who reports to Vaughn.

n2.speaker: Zara
n2.text: Heads up. The kitchen is talking about you and the corner office. I'm not asking. I'm telling you so you're not blindsided.

n3.text: An HR meeting appears in your calendar. Marcus is already in the room when you arrive.

n4.speaker: Marcus
n4.text: I've told HR the facts. We shared a taxi in a storm after a work event. I've also told them, voluntarily, that if anything ever changes, I'll declare it before it does.

choices.text: Back him up calmly, with the same facts.
'This is Vaughn. He's trying to get to Marcus through me.'

calm.text: HR closes the file in ten minutes. Outside, Marcus exhales for what seems like the first time all week.

n7.speaker: Marcus
n7.text: You handled that better than most directors would. ...I meant what I said in there. About declaring it. Before, not after.

accuse.text: HR goes very still and writes something down. Marcus closes his eyes for just a second.

n9.speaker: Marcus
n9.text: You're not wrong. But you can't win that fight in that room. Next time, let me take the hit. That's my job.

end.text: It blows over. Mostly. People look at the two of you slightly longer than they used to.

n1.text: Week 10. Marcus asks you to the rooftop. It's the first time he's ever asked you anywhere that isn't a meeting room.

n2.speaker: Marcus
n2.text: The CFO has offered me a director role. Strategy, two floors up. After launch I wouldn't run Lighthouse anymore. Someone else would. I wouldn't manage you.

n3.speaker: Marcus
n3.text: I haven't said yes. I wanted to ask you first, which is a very unprofessional sentence, and I'm saying it anyway.

choices.text: 'Take it because it's right for you. Not because of me.'
'Take it. Then ask me to dinner.'
'Stay. Lighthouse needs you more than strategy does.'

right.speaker: Marcus
right.text: It is right for me. I've known that for a year. I just needed someone to say it was allowed. ...You keep giving me permission to be a person.

dinner.speaker: Marcus
dinner.text: ...That is the most direct thing anyone has ever said to me on this roof. Ask me again after launch. I suspect the answer will be yes.

stay.speaker: Marcus
stay.text: Maybe. Or maybe it needs someone new. Someone like you. Think about that before you tell me to stay.

end.text: The sun goes down behind the city. He doesn't check his phone once.

n1.text: Week 11. Launch week. Everything is on fire in the normal, survivable way. Marcus finds you at your desk at 7am.

n2.speaker: Marcus
n2.text: Whatever happens at the gala, I want you to know: you were the best hire I've made in a decade. That's not your manager talking. Well. It is. But it's also me.

choices.text: 'Save me a dance. Strictly professional.'
'Same to you. Best boss I've had. Also, the slides are down to eight bullets.'

dance.speaker: Marcus
dance.text: Strictly. I'll be counting the bullet points the whole time.

slides.speaker: Marcus
slides.text: Eight. I'm moved. Genuinely. That's solid.

end.text: The gala is next week. Whatever this is, it's waiting for you there.

n1.text: Week 12. The Gala. Lighthouse launches without a hitch. Two floors up, a new name plate reads 'Marcus, Director of Strategy.' Your reviews now go to someone else entirely.

n2.text: He declared it to HR on Monday, exactly as promised. Before, not after. The form took four minutes. He says it was the bravest four minutes of his career.

n3.speaker: Marcus
n3.text: So. I'm not your manager. I've checked twice. HR has checked three times. Would you like to have dinner with me? Not a meeting. No slides.

n4.text: You say yes. He laughs like a man who's been holding his breath since a taxi in the rain.

n5.text: ♥ ROMANCE ENDING: 'Before, Not After.' You waited until it was right, and it was worth the wait. Thanks for playing Marcus's route.

n1.text: Week 12. The Gala. Marcus stayed on Lighthouse. You stayed on his team. Everything the two of you feel is still there, standing politely on the right side of a line.

n2.speaker: Marcus
n2.text: One dance. Strictly professional. ...I'm not good at this part. Waiting. But I'd rather wait than put a question mark next to anything you earn.

n3.text: You dance. You don't kiss. Something in the way he says goodnight sounds like 'not yet' rather than 'no.'

n4.text: ♡ BITTERSWEET ENDING: 'Not Yet.' Close, so close. The door is open, if either of you is ever brave enough to change the org chart. Thanks for playing Marcus's route.

n1.text: Week 12. The Gala. Marcus raises a glass to the new Lighthouse team, then stops beside you.

n2.speaker: Marcus
n2.text: I've put your name forward for the leadership programme. I'll sponsor you. Whatever you need — a reference, a hard conversation, a slide with fewer than twenty-three bullets — you have my number.

n3.text: It isn't romance. It's something rarer in this building: someone senior who is completely on your side.

n4.text: ▲ CAREER ENDING: 'That's Solid.' You gained a mentor for life. Thanks for playing Marcus's route.

n1.text: Week 12. The Gala. Marcus gives a gracious speech, thanks the team by name, and shakes your hand like he shakes everyone's.

n2.text: Whatever almost started on that rooftop never quite did. He's a good manager. You're a good employee. That's all it ever needed to be, apparently.

n3.text: ○ ENDING: 'Professional Distance.' Some lines stay uncrossed. Thanks for playing Marcus's route.

n1.speaker: Marcus
n1.text: Back-to-back meetings until six, I'm afraid. Leave it in my inbox and I'll give it real attention tonight.

n1.speaker: Marcus
n1.text: Lunch on Thursday? I found a place with no whiteboards. It's very relaxing. Slightly unsettling.
